title: In-Place String Compression
summary: Encoding and decoding run-length compression directly into a mutable character buffer, using a read cursor and a lagging write cursor that never overtakes it.

slides.markdown:
Run-length compression replaces a run of repeated characters with the character plus a count — `"aaabbc"` becomes `"a3b2c1"`. Doing this **in place**, writing the compressed form directly back over the original buffer, is the classic version interviewers ask for, and it hinges on one mechanism: a read cursor that scans ahead counting a run, and a lagging write cursor, always at or behind it, that writes the encoded form.

The cursor never overtaking the reader is what makes this safe — write past where you've already read, and you overwrite data you haven't looked at yet.

slides.sectionTitle: From immutable string to mutable buffer
slides.markdown:
"In place" only makes sense on something mutable. Since strings are immutable in most languages (covered earlier in this group), the very first step of any in-place string algorithm is converting to a mutable form — a `char[]` in Java, a `list` of characters in Python — before any read/write-cursor logic can run at all.

This conversion itself is O(n) and is a one-time, unavoidable cost; it's the operations *after* it that are the actual point of "in place" — no further allocation once you're working in the buffer.

slides.subTitle: Counting repeats, writing char+count
slides.markdown:
The encoding rule: scan the buffer, find each maximal run of identical consecutive characters, and write that character once followed by its count. `"aaabbbbcc"` → `"a3b4c2"`; a run of length 1 (`"c"` with no repeat) writes as `"c1"`, not just `"c"` — every run gets an explicit count, with no special case for singles.

The count is the entire value of this technique: a run of 1,000 identical characters compresses to just a few characters (the char plus its count's digits), while a run of 1 or 2 characters actually gets *longer* after encoding — which is exactly the trade-off examined a few slides ahead.

slides.sectionTitle: Read cursor counting, write cursor lagging
slides.markdown:
![A read pointer counting each run while a lagging write pointer overwrites the buffer in place with the compressed form](assets/compression-read-write-cursors.svg)

The read cursor does the counting work, advancing through an entire run before the write cursor commits anything for it. The write cursor only ever writes into positions the read cursor has already fully passed — that ordering guarantee is what keeps the in-place write from corrupting data still waiting to be read.

assets.alt: A read pointer counting each run while a lagging write pointer overwrites the buffer in place with the compressed form

slides.markdown:
```python
def compress(chars):
    write = 0
    read = 0
    n = len(chars)
    while read < n:
        char = chars[read]
        count = 0
        while read < n and chars[read] == char:
            read += 1
            count += 1
        chars[write] = char
        write += 1
        if count > 1:
            for digit in str(count):
                chars[write] = digit
                write += 1
    return write   # new logical length; chars[:write] is the compressed result
```

The read cursor fully consumes one run before the write cursor commits anything for it — count first, write after. This is O(n) time (each character is read exactly once) and O(1) extra space beyond the input buffer itself.

A run of 9 or fewer repeats has a single-digit count, and writing it as one character slot works cleanly. A run of 10 or more (`"aaaaaaaaaaa"`, 11 a's) has a **multi-digit** count — `"11"` needs two character slots, not one.

Code that assumes `count` always fits in a single output character (`chars[write] = str(count)` without iterating over each digit) silently drops digits or writes a malformed string the moment a run reaches double digits. The fix is writing the count digit by digit, as the implementation above does with `for digit in str(count)`, so a two- or three-digit count correctly occupies two or three slots.

If a run's encoded form (character plus multi-digit count) ever takes **more** slots than the run itself occupied in the original buffer, the write cursor can advance past where the read cursor currently is — and now the write is corrupting characters the read cursor hasn't examined yet, silently feeding the rest of the parse garbage input.

For single-character runs this can't happen (worst case, writing `char + "1"` for a run of length 1 takes 2 slots for 1 consumed — which is already a problem, covered next). The invariant to maintain: never let `write` exceed `read` at any point mid-algorithm. Any implementation that doesn't explicitly reason about this ordering is one edge case away from reading corrupted data it just wrote itself.

slides.sectionTitle: When compression actually shrinks the string
slides.markdown:
A run of length 1 encodes to 2 characters (`char + "1"`) — **longer** than the original. A run of length 2 also encodes to 2 characters (`char + "2"`) — the same length. Only runs of length 3 or more actually shrink: a run of 3 encodes to 2 characters, a run of 9 encodes to 2 characters, a run of 10 encodes to 3 characters (still shorter than 10).

This is exactly why the interview version of this problem is usually specified as "return the compressed string only if it's shorter than the original, otherwise return the original unchanged" — a string of mostly non-repeating characters (`"abcdef"`) would come out of blind run-length encoding *longer*, doubling in size instead of compressing. Checking the compressed length against the original length before committing to the compressed form is part of the actual solution, not an afterthought.

Decoding reverses the process: walk the compressed string reading a character, then reading the digits that follow it (there can be more than one, per the multi-digit pitfall above) until the next non-digit character, converting those digits to a count, and writing the character that many times into the output.

```python
def decompress(s):
    result = []
    i, n = 0, len(s)
    while i < n:
        char = s[i]
        i += 1
        j = i
        while j < n and s[j].isdigit():
            j += 1
        count = int(s[i:j])
        result.append(char * count)
        i = j
    return ''.join(result)
```

Note the digit-reading loop (`while s[j].isdigit()`) — this is exactly the multi-digit case from the pitfall, handled correctly on the way back out.

The read-cursor-ahead, write-cursor-lagging shape here is a specific instance of a pattern that shows up across in-place array and string problems: a fast pointer that scans and decides, and a slow pointer that only advances when there's something confirmed to keep or write.

Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place, moving all zeroes to the end while preserving order, and this compression problem all share the same skeleton — read decides what's real, write commits it, and write never gets ahead of read. Recognizing "this is the same two-cursor shape as [in-place reversal](in-place-reversal-shifting-rotation)'s pointer techniques, just with unequal advance rates instead of converging from both ends" is what turns a memorized solution into a transferable pattern.

slides.subTitle: And where it doesn't
slides.markdown:
Run-length encoding is a genuinely used technique in production, but only on data with long, real runs: simple bitmap image formats (fax transmission, some BMP variants), sparse boolean masks, and columnar database storage where a column repeats the same value across many consecutive rows. On that kind of data, RLE is close to optimal and essentially free to compute.

It does almost nothing for typical English text or source code, where runs of 3+ identical consecutive characters are rare — that's exactly why production text/general-purpose compressors (gzip, zstd) use entropy coding and dictionary-based matching (Huffman coding, LZ77-style back-references) instead, which exploit repeated *patterns* rather than repeated *single characters*. Knowing which category your data falls into — long literal runs vs general text — is what tells you whether reaching for RLE is a smart move or a five-minute detour that won't compress anything.
